subtype: Approach: asking what need the phone is meeting [Thinking]
passage: Dear Rekha, you asked why I've been so tired lately. I did something new: I asked myself why I scroll at night. I wrote down the honest answers on paper. One: it's lonely after everyone goes to bed, and the phone feels like company. Two: I'm dodging the maths homework because it makes my stomach tight. Neither is really about videos. So I made a plan with real replacements. On Thursdays I'd like to phone a friend at nine, and I was hoping that friend might be you. And I'll begin homework in ten-minute pieces, just ten, then a break. Would you mind being my nine o'clock call? I'll understand if not. — Vasudha

qa.q: What two things did Vasudha find behind the night scrolling?
qa.a: Loneliness after everyone goes to bed and dodging the maths homework.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel about this discovery?
qa.a: A mix of relief and sadness: naming the loneliness explained the scrolling and made a plan easier to write.

qa.q: What else could Vasudha try, and why?
qa.a: Start with a ten-minute homework goal at a fixed time, since a small start lowers the dread that sends Vasudha to the phone.

qa.q: How does the request look to Rekha?
qa.a: Rekha may feel touched and trusted, though Rekha will also need to decide whether that time can be given every Thursday.

grounding: A student asks why the scrolling happens at night, sees loneliness and homework worry, and plans real replacements.

subtype: Approach: asking what need the phone is meeting [Thinking]
passage:
Zainab, you asked on the student podcast how I cut down my night scrolling. I'm Dolma, and here's the honest answer: I stopped asking how to stop, and asked why I was doing it.
One night I wrote down what I felt right before I picked up the phone. Three nights running, it was the same two things. First, lonely. We'd moved to Delhi in June and I didn't really have anyone yet. Second, homework dread. The maths I hadn't started sat on the desk like a rock, and scrolling meant I didn't have to look at it.
So the phone was doing two jobs, badly. I gave those jobs to better things. For lonely: I call my old friend in Gangtok at nine, ten minutes, voice only. For dread: I open the maths and set a ten-minute timer. Just ten. Usually I keep going.
I still scroll sometimes. Just not till two.

qa.q: When does Dolma call the old friend in Gangtok?
qa.a: At nine, for ten minutes, voice only.

qa.q: What two feelings did Dolma find before picking up the phone?
qa.a: Dolma felt lonely after the move to Delhi, and full of dread about the maths homework.

qa.q: What else could Dolma do about the loneliness in Delhi?
qa.a: Join one club or activity at the new school, so there are people nearby to talk to as well as the old friend.

qa.q: How might the old friend in Gangtok feel about the nine o'clock calls?
qa.a: The friend probably enjoys staying close and feels valued, perhaps without knowing the calls replaced scrolling.

grounding: Shows a student asking what the night scrolling is for, finding loneliness and homework dread, and planning a friend call and ten-minute homework starts instead.

subtype: Approach: asking what need the phone is meeting [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Deepak, and Pallavi and I share a room, so I see her phone light up the ceiling most nights. Until last month it glowed till one.
Then one evening she sat on the bed with a notebook and asked me something odd: “When do you think I pick it up?” I said, “When you're bored?” She shook her head and wrote for a while. Later I saw the page. Two words circled: “alone” and “tests”.
She said it out loud, more to herself than to me: “I scroll when I miss my Mumbai friends, and when I'm scared to start chemistry.”
Now, around nine, she calls someone called Hina and laughs for ten minutes. Then she sets a kitchen timer for ten minutes and starts chemistry. The timer rings; usually she ignores it and keeps going.
The ceiling's been dark by eleven most nights. I don't know if she's less lonely. She seems lighter, though.

qa.q: What two words were circled on Pallavi's page?
What does Pallavi saying "I scroll when I miss my Mumbai friends" reveal?
qa.a: It shows she felt lonely and scared about chemistry, and had worked out that the phone was covering those feelings.

qa.q: What else could Pallavi try if the call and the timer stop working?
qa.a: Talk to a teacher or the school counsellor about settling in, so the loneliness gets real support beyond one call a night.

qa.q: How does the change look to Deepak?
qa.a: Deepak notices the ceiling dark by eleven and Pallavi seeming lighter, though Deepak can't be sure how she feels inside.

grounding: Someone sharing her room sees a student work out that she scrolls from loneliness and fear of starting chemistry, and replace it with a friend call and a timer.
